sec: Hyponatremia · regulators, classification, causes and hypovolemic hyponatremia

items.q: Fill up: The opening of the hyponatremia page names three regulators of water balance — the proximal convoluted tubule, the ______, and ADH, the last of which is annotated as ______.
opts: Loop of Henle and V1 receptor; maximal
items.exp: The three regulators listed are PCT, TAL (thick ascending limb)/DCT (distal convoluted tubule) and ADH, and ADH carries the annotation 'minimal'. (Book p962)

items.q: For the severity bands on Book p962, which serum sodium range defines the 'severe' category of hyponatremia?
items.exp: Severe is 100-119, moderate 120-129, mild 130-134 and very severe <100; the page prints these numbers with the unit mg/dL although sodium is expressed in mEq/L. (Book p962)

items.q: Assess the following about the classification of hyponatremia on Book p962: I The four bands are expressed in mg/dL rather than mEq/L. II A sodium of 96 falls in the band labelled 'severe'.
items.exp: The page does print mg/dL for mild 130-134, moderate 120-129, severe 100-119 and very severe <100; a sodium of 96 is therefore 'very severe', not 'severe'. (Book p962)

items.q: Match each serum sodium value with the severity band it occupies on this page — 1) 132 2) 124 3) 105 4) 96 … A) Mild B) Moderate C) Severe D) Very severe
items.exp: 130-134 is mild, 120-129 moderate, 100-119 severe and anything below 100 very severe hyponatremia. (Book p962)

items.q: Fill up: The first listed cause of hyponatremia is a central defect in thirst regulation due to ______, described as a water intake of about ______ per day.
items.exp: Cause 1 is a central defect in thirst regulation due to psychogenic polydipsia, with consumption of 15-20 L of water per day. (Book p962)

items.q: Every statement below fits the book's account of diuretic-induced hyponatremia EXCEPT:
opts: Loop diuretics block the DCT and cause hyponatremia more often than thiazides
Thiazide produces hyponatremia more than loop diuretics
The blocked segment is the distal convoluted tubule
Once the diluting segment is blocked, ADH continues to act
items.exp: The hierarchy is the reverse: thiazide > loop diuretics, because thiazides block the DCT so that ADH continues to act and hyponatremia follows. (Book p962)

items.q: A 66-year-old woman on hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension presents with a serum sodium of 123 mEq/L and normal renal function. Nephron-wise, which segment's blockade explains her hyponatremia?
items.exp: Thiazides act on the DCT; blocking this diluting segment leaves ADH free to act, which is the mechanism the page gives for thiazide hyponatremia. (Book p962)

items.q: Match each route of sodium loss in hypovolemic hyponatremia with its examples in the tree — 1) Renal loss 2) GI loss 3) 3rd space loss … A) Diarrhea, vomiting B) Tubular injury, mineralocorticoid insufficiency, cerebral salt wasting C) Burns, pancreatitis
items.exp: Renal loss lists tubular injury, mineralocorticoid insufficiency and CSW; GI loss lists diarrhea and vomiting; third-space loss lists burns and pancreatitis. (Book p962)

items.q: In the increased-ADH branch, hypervolemic hyponatremia is attributed to which haemodynamic abnormality and which two exemplars?
opts: Decreased effective volume — congestive cardiac failure and cirrhosis
Decreased true circulating volume — diarrhea and vomiting
Increased true circulating volume — acute nephritis and transfusion
items.exp: The tree separates reduced circulating (true) volume, which gives hypovolemic hyponatremia, from reduced effective volume, which gives hypervolemic hyponatremia in CCF and cirrhosis. (Book p962)

items.q: Assess the two findings listed for hypovolemic hyponatremia: I A reduced IVC diameter with tachycardia and postural hypotension is expected. II Urine output rises while skin turgor is preserved.
items.exp: The listed findings are reduced IVC diameter with tachycardia and postural hypotension, together with reduced urine output and reduced skin turgor. (Book p962)

items.q: A hyponatremic, volume-depleted man has a urine sodium of 38 mEq/L and a urine potassium of 30 mEq/L. Per the findings table, this electrolyte pattern indicates which cause?
opts: A purely renal cause without tubular damage
items.exp: Urine Na+ and K+ both above 20 mEq/L is the row assigned to tubular injury; Na+ >20 with K+ <10 is the row for mineralocorticoid insufficiency/CSW. (Book p962)

items.q: Match each urine electrolyte finding in the hypovolemic table with its cause — 1) Urine Na+ >20 mEq/L 2) Urine Na+ and K+ both >20 mEq/L 3) Urine Na+ >20 with K+ <10 mEq/L … A) Renal B) Tubular injury C) Mineralocorticoid insufficiency/CSW
items.exp: The three rows read: urine Na+ >20 as a renal cause, urine Na+ and K+ >20 as tubular injury, and urine Na+ >20 with K+ <10 as mineralocorticoid insufficiency or CSW. (Book p962)

items.q: Fill up: SIADH and cortisol or thyroid hormone insufficiency appear under the heading of ______ ADH and are the two entries given for ______ hyponatremia.
items.exp: Branch 3b is 'Inappropriate ADH', and the two causes listed beneath it — cortisol/thyroid hormone insufficiency and SIADH — produce euvolemic hyponatremia. (Book p962)

items.q: Assess the two severity lists in this volume: I This hyponatremia page caps mild at 134, whereas the ADH chapter's classification table caps mild at 135. II Both pages use identical upper limits for every band.
items.exp: Book p962 gives mild as 130-134 while Book p959 gave 130-135; moderate, severe and very severe bands agree, so the two lists are not identical. (Book p962)

items.q: All of the following are grouped under the renal loss arm of hypovolemic hyponatremia EXCEPT:
items.exp: Renal loss lists tubular injury, mineralocorticoid insufficiency and cerebral salt wasting; vomiting is placed under GI loss along with diarrhea. (Book p962)
